scenes.visual: Title card 'A Photo That Tells Time' over a camera shutter closing on a strip of boxy plant cells. COLOUR MAP (both films): chromosomes RED, BLUE, GREEN, YELLOW, each one thin thread before copying, two thin joined threads after copying in interphase, and a thick compact X only once coiled (prophase onward); cell membrane soft PEACH outline, nucleus pale GREY circle, plant cell wall DARK GREEN box outline; two on-screen counters top right, white text on charcoal: 'chromosomes: N' and 'copies: N'. All cells are cartoons labelled 'schematic'. Stage tally bars use one TEAL colour; any number appears only as on-screen text.

scenes.tts: Can a still photo tell you how long something takes? A photo freezes one moment, and nothing in it moves. So where would the time be hiding?
scenes.visual: A camera shutter clicks; a moving scene of a clock and a bouncing ball freezes into a still photo. A question card: 'how long?'
scenes.narration: Can a still photo tell you how long something takes? A photo freezes one moment, and nothing in it moves. So where would the time be hiding?

scenes.tts: The first film followed one model cell through the cycle, step by step, in order. A stained root tip cannot show you that. It gives you only a snapshot.
scenes.visual: Brief replay: the first film's cell with RED, BLUE, GREEN, YELLOW chromosomes running through the stage strip. Then a camera flash and the moving cell is replaced by a still photo of many cells, each frozen at a different point. Label 'snapshot'.
scenes.narration: The first film followed one model cell through the cycle, step by step, in order. A stained root tip cannot show you that. It gives you only a snapshot.

scenes.tts: Picture a huge school with no shared bell. Each student keeps a different timetable. Snap a photo at a random moment. Most students are in class. Only a few are in the hallway. Why?
scenes.visual: Cartoon cross-section of a school building, labelled 'schematic'. Each classroom has its own small clock showing a different time, label 'no shared bell'. Classrooms full of small figures; a hallway with three figures walking. A camera flash freezes the scene.
scenes.narration: Picture a huge school with no shared bell. Each student keeps a different timetable. Snap a photo at a random moment. Most students are in class. Only a few are in the hallway. Why?

scenes.tts: Class lasts much longer than the walk between classes. So at any random moment, a student is more likely to be in class.
scenes.visual: A timeline bar under the school: a long block labelled 'class' and a short block labelled 'hallway', repeating. A moving cursor drops randomly onto the bar again and again; most drops land in 'class' blocks, shown by small dots piling up.
scenes.narration: Class lasts much longer than the walk between classes. So at any random moment, a student is more likely to be in class.

scenes.tts: Try it yourself. Stage A lasts twice as long as Stage B. In a random snapshot, which stage will you see more of?
scenes.caption: Try it yourself. Stage A lasts twice as long as Stage B. In a random snapshot, which stage will you see more of?
scenes.visual: Two bars side by side: 'Stage A' twice the length of 'Stage B', labelled 'time A = 2 x time B'. Pause card: 'In a snapshot, more A or more B?'
scenes.narration: Try it yourself. Stage A lasts twice as long as Stage B. In a random snapshot, which stage will you see more of?

scenes.visual: Predict pause. Question card holds; 5-second ring timer at bottom right.

scenes.tts: Stage A. You should see about twice as many things in Stage A. A stage that lasts longer tends to hold more of them in a snapshot.
scenes.visual: Dots rain onto the two bars at random. A counter under each fills; A ends near twice B, with on-screen text 'about 2 : 1'. These dots are a computed random simulation, labelled 'computed: random moments'.
scenes.narration: Stage A. You should see about twice as many things in Stage A. A stage that lasts longer tends to hold more of them in a snapshot.

scenes.tts: Now swap the students for cells. Set an onion on a glass of water, and roots grow down. Near each root tip, cells divide often.
scenes.visual: Cartoon onion sitting on a glass of water; white roots grow downward in time-lapse. A circle highlights a region near one root tip, labelled 'near the root tip: cells divide often'.
scenes.narration: Now swap the students for cells. Set an onion on a glass of water, and roots grow down. Near each root tip, cells divide often.

scenes.tts: A thin root tip is dyed, or stained, so the chromosomes show up. Under a microscope, each cell is caught at one moment of its own cycle.
scenes.visual: The root tip slides under a cartoon microscope. A purple stain washes over it. The view fills with boxy plant cells with DARK GREEN walls; most show a plain grey nucleus, a few show coloured chromosomes. Label 'schematic, not the real counts'.
scenes.narration: A thin root tip is dyed, or stained, so the chromosomes show up. Under a microscope, each cell is caught at one moment of its own cycle.

scenes.tts: Each cell is sorted into a stage by what its chromosomes look like. Thick, coiled chromosomes, not yet in a row, mean prophase. A row across the middle means metaphase.
scenes.visual: Two cells pop out of the grid. One holds thick coiled Xs in RED, BLUE, GREEN, YELLOW, scattered and not in a row, and drops into a bin labelled 'prophase'. The other holds the same Xs in a row across its middle and drops into a bin labelled 'metaphase'. Same shapes and colours as the first film.
scenes.narration: Each cell is sorted into a stage by what its chromosomes look like. Thick, coiled chromosomes, not yet in a row, mean prophase. A row across the middle means metaphase.

scenes.tts: Let's work one stage together, using real counts. In one set of thirty-six photographed onion cells, ten were in prophase, the coiled stage.
scenes.caption: Let's work one stage together, using real counts. In one set of 36 photographed onion cells, 10 were in prophase, the coiled stage.
scenes.visual: A single TEAL tally bar labelled 'prophase' fills one block at a time to '10', against a grey outline marked '36 cells in all'. No other stage bar is shown.
scenes.narration: Let's work one stage together, using real counts. In one set of 36 photographed onion cells, 10 were in prophase, the coiled stage.

scenes.tts: Turn that count into a share of all the cells. Follow the steps on the screen. Prophase holds about twenty-eight percent of the cells.
scenes.caption: Turn that count into a share of all the cells. Follow the steps on the screen. Prophase holds about 28 percent of the cells.
scenes.visual: On-screen steps write themselves one line at a time: '10 / 36', '≈ 0.28', '≈ 28 percent'. A pie of 36 small wedges shades 10 of them TEAL.
scenes.narration: Turn that count into a share of all the cells. Follow the steps on the screen. Prophase holds about 28 percent of the cells.

scenes.tts: The activity says to assume one cycle takes twenty-four hours. Take each stage's share of the cells as its share of the time. Then prophase lasts about seven hours.
scenes.caption: The activity says to assume one cycle takes 24 hours. Take each stage's share of the cells as its share of the time. Then prophase lasts about 7 hours.
scenes.visual: A 24-hour clock face labelled 'assumed: 24 hours'. A TEAL wedge sweeps 28 percent of it. On-screen steps: '28 percent of 24 hours', '= about 7 hours'.
scenes.narration: The activity says to assume one cycle takes 24 hours. Take each stage's share of the cells as its share of the time. Then prophase lasts about 7 hours.

scenes.tts: Treat this as a rough guide. There are only thirty-six photos, and nobody says how they were picked. And the twenty-four hours is assumed, not measured.
scenes.caption: Treat this as a rough guide. There are only 36 photos, and nobody says how they were picked. And the 24 hours is assumed, not measured.
scenes.visual: Two sticky notes slap onto the clock: 'only 36 photos; how picked? unknown' and '24 hours: assumed, not measured'. The '7 hours' label turns to 'about 7 hours?'
scenes.narration: Treat this as a rough guide. There are only 36 photos, and nobody says how they were picked. And the 24 hours is assumed, not measured.

scenes.tts: Still, it works best with many fairly picked cells, dividing out of step in a steadily growing root. Then a longer stage tends to hold more cells in a snapshot. So a stage's share of the cells is only a rough guide to its time.
scenes.visual: Return to the stained root-tip grid. Small clocks over a few cells show different times, label 'out of step'. A small note: 'many cells, fairly picked, steady growth'. Random camera flashes; a cursor on a cell-cycle timeline lands more often on longer arcs, shown with computed random dots, labelled 'computed: random moments'. Arc lengths are labelled 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Still, it works best with many fairly picked cells, dividing out of step in a steadily growing root. Then a longer stage tends to hold more cells in a snapshot. So a stage's share of the cells is only a rough guide to its time.

scenes.tts: That was one stage. Four more are waiting, along with the biggest question in the lesson. Now count the rest yourself.
scenes.visual: Four empty TEAL bars appear beside the filled prophase bar, labelled 'interphase', 'metaphase', 'anaphase', 'telophase', each with a question mark. A pencil icon appears.
scenes.narration: That was one stage. Four more are waiting, along with the biggest question in the lesson. Now count the rest yourself.

scenes.visual: End card with Hex holding a camera and a stained root-tip photo. Line: 'Out of step, a longer stage tends to hold more cells.'
